children: Nvidia

recorded its sixth consecutive weekly drop this week amid a broader selloff in the U.S. tech sector, adding to the sharp losses the company recorded in October, which also happened to be its worst monthly decline for this year. With its share price approaching levels not seen since April, Seeking Alpha analysts reviewed their positions on the stock, triggering a healthy conversation around its valuation.
The Bulls
“Nvidia Corporation is a Strong Buy after a 20% selloff, with current sentiment-driven declines presenting a compelling entry point,” wrote SA analyst
in

params.linkText: “Here's Why I Bought Nvidia While The Market Cried In Fear (Rating Upgrade).”

children: Even under conservative growth assumptions, NVDA's fair value ranges from $156 to $252 per share, offering significant upside versus current levels.
“NVDA stock trades at just over 13x FY28 EPS targets, not reflecting sustainable growth prospects fueled by SpaceX's commitments,” noted Seeking Alpha Investing Group Leader
in
“Nvidia: SpaceX Offers An Ignored Bonus.”
“Nvidia Corporation is set up to get a large bonus via SpaceX's massive AI data center plans, providing a significant growth catalyst.”
“NVDA's 70% projected revenue growth and 74% gross margins are underpinned by robust AI demand and supply constraints, not demand limitations.,” added Index Analyst in
“Nvidia: Competitive Moat Widening; Buy.”
“At $301.53 per share of valuation, there's a possible upside of 46% from the current share price of $206.”
“The selloff on Oct. 30 was triggered by something other than Nvidia,” argued SA analyst Benjamin C. Barry in
“Nvidia: Trade The Fear With NVDL.”
“That means the poor performance from Intel and nervousness in the credit markets wiped about $220 billion from Nvidia's valuation, despite the fact that Nvidia had just raised its own outlook.”
“Nvidia’s biggest problem right now is that customers want more than it can make, and frankly, that’s a good problem to have,” wrote Rick Orford in
“Nvidia May Actually Raise Its 70% Growth Guide In November.”
“The stock also costs less today than when I last talked about it, and I’m comfortable with that setup as long as the second answer doesn’t turn ugly.”
The Bears
“NVDA trades at a 17.7x 1-yr fwd P/E, below semiconductor peers and its historical average, creating a valuation counterweight,” opined SA analyst Hunting Alphas in
“Nvidia: Time To Lock In The Profits.”
“Vera Rubin adoption and rising B200 rental rates support Nvidia’s growth outlook, creating upside risks despite pressure on margins and cash conversion.”
“My valuation model implies NVDA is overvalued by 11%, with significant downside if financing constraints and competitive pressures persist into FY28,” wrote Bears of Wall Street in
“Nvidia: Brace For The Worst.”
“We believe that the bearish thesis has only strengthened, and Nvidia’s stock has plenty of room to fall.”
“Despite the CDS widening by 80 bps since July, NVDA's share price has risen 12%, highlighting a stark disconnect between credit and equity markets,” argued Stuart Allsopp in
“Nvidia: Equity Investors Are Ignoring The Surge In Implied Default Risk.”
“To justify an equity position, NVDA must deliver at least a 6.7% annual return for 30 years, requiring sustained free cash flow growth and sustained multiples.”
“On paper, Nvidia is cheaper on a growth-adjusted basis than it has been for most of the past five years,” wrote The Techie in
“Nvidia: Jensen Can't Spend His Way Out Of This One.”
“However, that multiple only holds if the growth estimates hold, and custom silicon, China share loss, and stressed neocloud customers are precisely the risks to those estimates.”

title: Bulls vs. Bears: NVIDIA sparks valuation debate as stock nears six-month low
